Get started with fasttrop

Source: vignettes/fasttrop.Rmd
fasttrop.Rmd

This vignette shows a first analysis with fasttrop. You make a practice panel, you calculate the TROP estimate, and you read the result. The article “TROP in plain words” on the package website explains the ideas of the method.

The data

fasttrop uses panel data in long format. Each row is one unit in one period. The data must have four columns:

  • the outcome
  • the treatment indicator, with the values 0 and 1
  • the unit identifier
  • the period identifier

The function trop_simulate() makes a practice panel with a known effect. In this panel, 5 of 20 units get the treatment in the last 3 of 12 periods. The true effect is 1 for each treated cell.

library(fasttrop)
panel <- trop_simulate(n_units = 20, n_periods = 12, n_treated = 5, n_post = 3,
                       effect = 1, seed = 1)
head(panel)
#>   unit time          y d         y0
#> 1    1    1 -0.5496887 0 -0.5496887
#> 2    2    1 -0.5309372 0 -0.5309372
#> 3    3    1 -1.1621093 0 -1.1621093
#> 4    4    1  2.5570765 0  2.5570765
#> 5    5    1 -0.1638954 0 -0.1638954
#> 6    6    1 -1.1801013 0 -1.1801013

The column y is the outcome, and the column d is the treatment indicator. The column y0 is the outcome without the treatment. Real data does not have this column. The practice panel has it, so you can compare the estimate with the truth.

A first estimate

To calculate the estimate, give trop() the data and the names of the four columns. In this first fit, you set the tuning parameters. This makes the fit fast.

fit <- trop(panel, outcome = "y", treatment = "d", unit = "unit", time = "time",
            lambda = c(time = 0.2, unit = 0.5, nn = 0.5), n_boot = 100, seed = 1)
fit
#> Triply Robust Panel (TROP) estimate
#>   Method: local | Design: block | Units: 20 | Periods: 12 | Treated cells: 15
#>   ATT: 1.119  (SE 0.2199, 95% CI 0.6879 to 1.55)
#>   lambda: time = 0.2, unit = 0.5, nn = 0.5

After the title, the output has three lines:

  1. The method, the design of the panel, the size of the panel, and the number of treated cells.
  2. The average treatment effect on the treated (ATT), with the bootstrap standard error (SE) and the 95% confidence interval.
  3. The tuning parameters.

The true ATT of this panel is 1. The interval contains this value.

Parts of the result

Use these functions to get parts of the result:

coef(fit)
#>      ATT 
#> 1.118779
confint(fit)
#>         2.5 %   97.5 %
#> ATT 0.6878718 1.549686
head(as.data.frame(fit))
#>   unit time        tau
#> 1    7   10  2.0694817
#> 2    7   11  3.3467710
#> 3    7   12  0.1396825
#> 4   11   10  0.7607983
#> 5   11   11  1.9304028
#> 6   11   12 -0.3167042

The function as.data.frame() gives the effect for each treated cell. The ATT is the mean of these effects.

Let the data select the tuning parameters

TROP has three tuning parameters:

  • time sets how fast the time weights decrease with the distance from the treated period. With 0, all periods get the same weight.
  • unit sets how fast the unit weights decrease when the outcome history of a unit is different from the treated unit. With 0, all units get the same weight.
  • nn is the penalty on the low-rank term. A larger value gives a simpler low-rank term. With Inf, the model has no low-rank term.

If you do not set lambda, cross-validation selects the tuning parameters from the grid of trop_grid(). To make this example fast, the cross-validation uses a sample of 60 untreated cells.

fit_cv <- trop(panel, outcome = "y", treatment = "d", unit = "unit", time = "time",
               cv_cells = 60, n_boot = 100, seed = 1)
summary(fit_cv)
#> Triply Robust Panel (TROP) estimate
#>   Method: local | Design: block | Units: 20 | Periods: 12 | Treated cells: 15
#>   ATT: 1.142  (SE 0.2267, 95% CI 0.6978 to 1.587)
#>   lambda: time = 0.1, unit = 0.5, nn = 1
#>   Tuning: loocv, score 18.79, 34 grid evaluations
#>   Bootstrap: 100 draws (stratified), 0 failed, normal interval
#>   Treated units: 5 | Skipped cells: 0 | Non-converged fits: 0
#>   Time: 1.572 s in total, 1.568 s in the C code (2 threads)

The function summary() also gives the result of the tuning, the bootstrap, and the time of the calculation. With cv_cells = NULL, the default, the cross-validation uses all untreated cells, as in the paper. This takes more time, but it uses all the data.

The local method and the global method

The default method is the local method of the paper. It calculates a separate fit for each treated cell. The global method is the method of the Python package from the authors. It calculates one fit for all treated cells. You can use the global method only for a block design. In a block design, all treated units start the treatment in the same period and stay treated.

fit_global <- trop(panel, outcome = "y", treatment = "d", unit = "unit",
                   time = "time", method = "global",
                   lambda = c(time = 0.2, unit = 0.5, nn = 0.5), n_boot = 100,
                   seed = 1)
coef(fit_global)
#>      ATT 
#> 1.156408

Standard errors and intervals

A unit bootstrap gives the standard error. Each draw takes a sample of units with replacement and calculates the estimate again. fasttrop keeps the tuning parameters fixed in each draw. The argument n_boot sets the number of draws. The default is 200 draws.

The default interval is a normal interval. To get a percentile interval, set ci = "percentile". The bootstrap is correct only with many treated units. For a panel with fewer than five treated units, fasttrop gives a warning message.

Threads and seeds

fasttrop runs its model fits in C, and it can use more than one thread. The function trop_threads() gives the default number of threads. To set the number of threads, use trop_control():

fit <- trop(panel, outcome = "y", treatment = "d", unit = "unit", time = "time",
            control = trop_control(threads = 4))

The number of threads does not change the results. With the same seed, a fit gives the same result each time. The seed argument does not change the random number generator of your R session.
